opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few big ones, and they kind of compound on each other.

The first is just the cost of building the tasks. For the time-horizon methodology, you need tasks where you have a reasonably good estimate of how long they take a skilled human, and ideally you actually have humans do them to get baselines. When tasks take a few minutes or an hour, that's manageable. When you're talking about tasks that take a human a full day, or a week, or a month, getting baselines becomes really expensive. You're paying experts for a lot of hours, and many attempts fail or get abandoned for reasons that have nothing to do with the task's difficulty. So the number of long tasks you can afford to build and baseline is much smaller, and your estimates at the long end get noisier.

The second is scoring. A lot of our shorter tasks have fairly crisp, automatic success criteria: the tests pass or they don't. As tasks get longer and more realistic, they tend to get messier. Real multi-day projects don't usually have a single unit test that tells you you're done. There are judgment calls about quality, maintainability, whether the thing actually solves the underlying problem. If you make the scoring fully automatic, you risk pushing toward artificially clean tasks that aren't representative of real long-horizon work. If you use human judgment, it gets expensive and you add noise and possible bias.

Related to that is a representativeness worry. To keep long tasks tractable to build and score, there's pressure to pick tasks that are well-specified and self-contained. But a lot of what makes real long work hard is ambiguity, coordinating with other people, gathering context, and recovering from wrong turns. So you could end up measuring a model's ability to do long, *tidy* tasks and extrapolating to messy real-world work in a way that overstates capability. We've tried to look at this with some "messiness" analyses, but it's a real limitation.

Then there's the running-the-agents side. Long tasks mean long agent runs: lots of tokens, lots of compute, more infrastructure that can break. Environment flakiness that's a minor annoyance on a ten-minute task becomes a serious source of error over a multi-hour run. And you need enough runs per task to get decent success-rate estimates.

Finally, there's a somewhat conceptual issue. The time-horizon metric relies on a fairly clean relationship where models succeed at short tasks and fail at long ones, and you fit a curve to find, say, the 50% point. As horizons extend, it's not obvious that human time-to-complete remains the right axis of difficulty. Some long tasks are long because they involve lots of routine steps, others because they require deep insight. Models might handle those very differently, so the single-number summary might become less meaningful the further out you go.

So I think the methodology is still useful and the trend is real, but as we push to longer tasks, the error bars widen, and we need to think harder about task design, scoring, and what exactly we're claiming when we report a horizon.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that it gets hard in a few different ways at once, and they kind of compound.

The first one is just task creation. The whole methodology depends on having tasks where we know how long they take humans, and for the short stuff, like tasks that take ten minutes or an hour, that's pretty tractable. You can pay people to do them, you get a decent distribution of completion times, you can calibrate. Once you're talking about tasks that take a human a week, or a month, it becomes enormously expensive to get even a single human baseline, let alone enough to have a meaningful estimate. And the people who are able to do a month-long software or research project are exactly the people whose time is most expensive and hardest to get. So the number of long tasks we have is small, and the error bars on the human time estimates are wide.

The second problem is what the tasks actually look like. When we build an evaluation task, we have to make it self-contained and automatically gradable. That's a pretty strong constraint. Real week-long work usually involves a lot of underspecification, going back to a person and asking what they actually want, discovering halfway through that the original framing was wrong. We mostly design that out, because you can't score it. So there's a real question of whether a "one week task" in our suite is representative of one week of real work, or whether it's a cleaner, more legible thing that happens to take a week. I think it's probably the latter to some degree, and that means the time horizon numbers might overstate how well these systems do on messy real-world work of the same nominal length.

Third, there's a measurement issue. The time horizon is defined as the task length where the model succeeds fifty percent of the time, and we fit a curve to get that. When the horizon is at the edge of or beyond the longest tasks we have, you're extrapolating, and the curve fit gets pretty sensitive to the few long data points you do have. So the uncertainty just grows as the horizon grows, structurally, not just because of noise.

And then there's a more conceptual thing, which is that the "time it takes a human" framing may start to break down. For short tasks, human time is a decent proxy for difficulty. For long tasks, a lot of what makes them long for a human isn't inherent difficulty, it's things like waiting on feedback, context switching, fatigue, coordination with other people. A model doesn't have those costs in the same way, so a task that takes a human a month might not actually be "a month hard" in any sense that's meaningful for a model. I don't think we have a great replacement metric yet, but I think as we push longer we're going to have to be more careful about what the number is actually claiming.

So, to summarize: expensive and scarce baselines, task realism, extrapolation uncertainty, and the metric itself getting less meaningful. None of those are fatal, but I think people should hold the long-horizon numbers with a fair amount of humility.

r002.rationale: It says month-long software or research tasks require people whose time is especially expensive and hard to obtain, identifying specialized human expertise as a baselining challenge.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest harvesting already-completed work as a way to make task-suite expansion affordable.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different challenges. One is just the cost of doing the evaluations. If you want to evaluate a task that takes a human several days, you need someone to actually do that task to establish the baseline. And you need enough tasks, and enough model runs, that you’re measuring something reasonably robust rather than whether the model happened to succeed on one particular problem.

Another is figuring out what the human time is really measuring. For longer tasks, there’s often a lot of context acquisition, or waiting for something, or interacting with other people. A task might take a week on the calendar without representing a week of focused work. So you need to be careful about how you interpret that as a measure of difficulty.

And then there’s the question of whether the tasks still look like the work you ultimately care about. It’s relatively easy to specify a bounded programming task with a clear success criterion. A lot of longer projects involve figuring out what the goal should be, getting feedback, and revising the plan. If you remove all of that to make the task easy to grade, you might lose something important. But if you leave it in, evaluation becomes much harder.

So I’d want to distinguish between extending the existing measurement to longer tasks and establishing that it captures the ability to carry out long, messy projects in the real world. Those are related, but the second requires more than just running the model for longer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cost and interpretation of longer tasks, but does not mention four-month doubling or the need to evaluate full-working-day tasks soon.

r002.rationale: It says a human must do longer tasks to establish a baseline, but does not identify specialized human expertise as a challenge.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest using tasks people have already completed to make the evaluation suite more affordable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few challenges. One is just the practical difficulty of finding tasks that take a human a long time, where we can still reliably determine whether the AI succeeded. You want the task to be long because there’s substantial work to do, rather than because someone is waiting for a process to finish, or because the instructions are ambiguous.

Another is measuring the human baseline. If a task takes an expert several days, getting multiple people to do it becomes quite expensive. And differences in their background knowledge can matter a lot. Someone who already knows a codebase might finish much faster than someone who has to learn it, so you have to be careful about what your time estimate actually means.

Then there’s the question of how representative the tasks are. You can construct a longer task by putting a bunch of short tasks together, but that might miss what’s difficult about real long projects: figuring out what to do, noticing that an approach isn’t working, and revising your plan. We’d want evaluations that capture those things, while still having a clear enough outcome that we can score them.

And finally, running the evaluations gets more expensive and harder to debug. When an agent fails after working for a very long time, you need to understand whether that tells you something about its capabilities or whether there was a problem with the environment. All of those issues get more consequential as you extend the horizon.
